implementation_notes: Ruby passes blocks implicitly to every method, so the pattern is a block (or an explicit Proc/lambda) that the owner yields to with the current state: the Proc documentation describes a Proc as an encapsulation of a block of code which can be stored in a local variable, passed to a method or another Proc, and called, and notes that lambdas are useful as self-sufficient functions and as arguments to higher-order functions. The classic component structure is replaced by yield or an &block parameter; Rails view components expose the same mechanism as content and slot blocks. Prefer the block form for call-site rendering, an explicit Proc when the renderer must be stored or called later, and a template/partial when the markup is better expressed declaratively.
code_sketch: def track_mouse loop do x, y = read_pointer yield(x, y) # caller decides the markup end end track_mouse { |x, y| "#{x},#{y}" }
pitfalls: A non-lambda block's return exits the defining method and a stored block that outlives its method raises LocalJumpError; use a lambda (-> {}) for renderers that are stored or invoked later.
Blocks are not objects unless captured with █ capturing on every call costs allocations in hot loops, and Symbol#to_proc is tempting where a real renderer with state is required.
Implicit blocks keep the rendering contract out of the signature; document the block arity or name the parameter explicitly so consumers know what the owner yields.
